steps: The grid has 8 × 5 = 40 shapes, but they are not all the same.
Sort them into types by their corners: rounded arms, square arms, mixed.
Count one type at a time, row by row, with a tally.
The most common type appears 14 times.

steps: Put Q at the origin: P(−2, 0), R(2, 0), S(0, 2). Both triangles PQS and QRS have area 2.
Line PS cuts the left semicircle along a chord that makes a 90° angle at its centre T.
The cap of the semicircle outside the triangle exactly balances the extra piece removed inside: each side shades exactly 1.
The right side works the same way: 1 + 1 = 2. No pi is left in the answer.

steps: Count each shape type separately, and mark each one lightly as you count.
Include triangles formed by two or more pieces, and rectangles hidden inside larger ones.
Count only full circles; arcs and semicircles are not circles.
Then calculate (triangles − circles) ÷ rectangles = 6.
qs.trap: Counting arcs as circles, or squares as "not rectangles". Every square is also a rectangle.

steps: The front view shows the hot cube sinking half its height into the top face, so it cuts a groove with a flat floor.
Follow the top view: the groove enters from the left, turns diagonally from Q to R, then exits on the right.
Count new faces part by part: the floor and side walls of each straight run, and the end wall at Q.
The original faces plus all new groove faces make 16.
qs.trap: Forgetting the faces at the turns. Every change of direction creates new wall faces.

steps: Look for pairs: most numbers have a "reversed" partner (57 and 75, 43 and 34, 18 and 81, 54 and 45).
Compare each pair in detail: the side of the drop, the drop position, the number.
One pot breaks the rule that its partner follows.
The official answer is the pot numbered 62.
qs.trap: Looking only at the numbers. In visual puzzles, the drawing details are part of the rule.

steps: A pattern is the design on the light half of the capsule: horizontal lines, vertical lines, a grid and so on.
Ignore how each capsule is turned. Rotate it in your head so the pattern is upright.
Write the list as you scan, adding only new patterns.
There are 4 different patterns.
qs.trap: Counting the same stripes twice when the capsule is turned 90°: horizontal becomes vertical.

steps: Start at one corner of the figure and work in a fixed order: ears, head, body, feet, tail and fork.
Watch for letters used as parts: an O as an eye, a Y as a whisker, repeated letters in the fork.
Write each letter on rough paper as you find it.
The total is 31.
qs.trap: Missing small letters inside bigger ones, or counting a rotated letter as a new shape.

steps: A pencil counts only if it has both a sharpened tip and an eraser at the other end.
Follow each pencil from end to end, even where it passes under others.
Reject pencils that are blunt, have no eraser, or have two tips.
8 pencils match P exactly.
qs.trap: Counting erasers or tips alone. Trace the full length of each pencil.

steps: A usable kettle needs a body that holds water, a spout or lip to pour, and a handle you can hold safely.
Check each kettle silhouette for all three features.
Reject designs that cannot pour (no spout) or cannot be held (no handle).
13 kettles pass all three checks.
qs.trap: Judging by style. A strange shape can still work; a familiar one can be missing its spout.

steps: P is a square split into 8 triangles by its diagonals and midlines.
Each piece carries part of a digit. Look for the right angle on each piece: it sits at the centre or a corner.
Join pieces whose black strokes continue across the edges.
The digits read 7, 4, 5.
qs.trap: Reading a piece upside down. Fix the orientation of one piece first, then build around it.

steps: A ring can rise only if it is cut free along its arcs and joined to the sheet only along a dotted fold line.
Check each ring: does it have a dotted hinge, and is it free elsewhere?
Rings with no hinge fall out; rings with no cut stay flat.
5 rings stand up.
qs.trap: Counting every drawn arc. A ring needs both a cut and a fold to stand.

steps: In landscape the screen is 10 cm wide and 4 cm tall.
The picture height shrinks from 10 to 4, a scale of 0.4. Its width becomes 4 × 0.4 = 1.6 cm.
Blank width = 10 − 1.6 = 8.4 cm, split equally: 4.2 cm on each side.
Left blank area = 4.2 × 4 = 16.8 cm².

steps: Equal layers of 1 cm marbles: 10 × 10 per layer, 10 layers, so 1000 marbles.
One marble: 4/3 × 22/7 × 0.5³ = 0.524 cm³. All marbles: about 523.8 cm³.
Tank volume = 1000 cm³.
Water = 1000 − 523.8 = 476.2 cm³, inside the accepted range.

steps: A pointed flexible nib makes thin lines with light pressure and thick lines when pressed.
So it can make an even thin line (A) and strokes that swell from thin to thick (B, C).
D has strokes that are evenly broad with square, flat ends, which needs a broad, flat-edged tool.
A, B and C are possible.
qs.trap: Assuming a pointed nib can only make thin lines. Pressure spreads the tines and thickens the stroke.

steps: Imagine the frame split by two vertical and two horizontal lines into 9 equal parts.
A photo follows the rule when its main subject sits on a line or where two lines cross.
In A, B and C the main subject (the boy, the seated figure, the monument) sits near a third line.
D places its subject centrally behind the fence, so it does not follow the rule.
qs.trap: Choosing any photo that "looks good". The rule is about where the subject sits.

steps: The strip repeats one unit across its length. Find one full repeat first.
Choose one clear feature in each option (a cross, an arrow-head, a diagonal bar).
Find that feature in the strip and check the area around it matches square by square.
A and D match parts of the strip; B and C do not.
qs.trap: Accepting a mirrored copy. A flipped piece looks similar but is not part of the strip.

note needs n and e: not available.
ghost and short use only h, r, s, o, g, t: both possible.
enter needs n and e: not available.

steps: The images are squeezed, tall versions of the text. Some are also mirrored or flipped.

steps: Track each element separately: the ringed circle, the dot inside it, the outer circle and the triangle.
Each one rotates or moves by a fixed step from figure to figure.
The missing figure must sit between its neighbours for every element.
Option B matches all four elements.
qs.trap: Tracking only the big shapes and ignoring the small dot, which decides between close options.

steps: Compare the same digits across boxes first: 1, 2 and 6 appear in every number.
Look at stroke ends, curves and the width of each digit.
Then compare the last digit's style with the others.
Box D (1265) uses a different font.
qs.trap: Comparing only the last digit. Compare the repeated digits first; they reveal the font.

steps: The logo is a knot of six identical interlocking loops, turning around an open centre.
Check the centre: open or filled?
Check the over-and-under weaving: each loop passes over one and under the next, all the same way.
Option D has the correct centre and weave.
qs.trap: Judging by overall shape. Logo questions test small details: centre, weave and spacing.

steps: Each ring keeps the part of the letters that fell inside it.
The outer ring keeps the outer tips of the letters; the middle ring and inner disc keep the middle parts.
Rotation can change the angle, but not which letter parts each piece holds.
Only C has the correct letter parts on every piece.
qs.trap: Expecting the pieces to sit at the same angle. The question says they were rotated.

steps: Each piece of P has a coloured corner (red or blue), a black part and a white part.
Rotate each option to match a quarter of P, checking colours at each edge and corner.
Edges must continue the black and white curves of the neighbouring piece.
C is a mirror image of a quarter, so it cannot fit.
qs.trap: Rotating C until it "almost" fits. A mirror image never matches by rotation.

steps: Rebuild the full shape first: a large triangle with rows of small triangles. Each row has 2 more than the row above.
Count the triangles in the full shape, row by row.
Count the triangles left, counting a partly bitten one as eaten.
Eaten = full − remaining = 25.
qs.trap: Counting only whole triangles as eaten. The question includes partial ones.

steps: A shadow points away from the Sun, and a long shadow means a low Sun.
P: shadow to the west, Sun in the east: morning (10:30 am).
R: shadow directly below: 12 noon. S: short shadow, slightly east: just after noon (1 pm).
Q: very long shadow to the east, Sun low in the west: evening (6 pm). That is D.

steps: Work backwards: start from each baby on the right and trace the path to the left.
At crossings, the paths go over and under; do not turn.
Mark the path with your pencil as you go.
Only parent B's path reaches its own baby (the blue fish).
qs.trap: Turning at a crossing. In weaving mazes, paths cross over each other without joining.

steps: A capital T has a straight top bar centred on a straight stem.
Scan in horizontal strips, left to right, and tick each T you find.
Count a T even when it is turned or upside down, but not an L or a plus sign, which only look similar.
The total is 16.
qs.trap: Counting the same T twice at the edge of two strips. Overlap your strips slightly and keep ticks.

steps: Each letter becomes one digit: vowel = 1, consonant = 0.
Check: d-e-l-u-l-u gives 0 1 0 1 0 1. It works.
010100 needs 6 letters: consonant, vowel, consonant, vowel, consonant, consonant.
m-e-w-i-n-g fits. boujee (011011) and pookie (011010) do not.

steps: The missing part must fill every gap exactly: long teeth where the black is short, and short teeth where it is long.
Turn the options in your mind so their teeth point up into the black figure.
Compare three or four distinctive teeth (the longest and shortest) first.
Only C matches every tooth.
qs.trap: Matching the outline only. Every single tooth must line up.

S: a faded Jain mural, Sittanavasal (Tamil Nadu).

steps: Group the letters by font features: serifs, stroke contrast, weight, width.
One group is a classic serif (book-style) font: d, e, l, i, g, h, t.
Check each option word against that group.
Only delight uses letters all from one font.
qs.trap: Grouping by size. Letters of the same font can appear at different sizes.

steps: A curved glass full of water acts like a lens.
Through the straight middle the stripes look almost straight, just magnified.
Through the rounded bottom of the bowl the stripes bend into curves.
Option B shows straight lines above and curved lines near the bottom.
qs.trap: Expecting all lines to curve the same way. The bending depends on the curve of the glass at each height.

steps: Each car strip turns about its fixed pivot like a see-saw.
If the fixed pivot is above the push strip, the car moves opposite to the push. If it is below, the car moves with the push.
In B one fixed pivot is above and the other below, so the cars move in opposite directions and meet when the strip is pulled.
In A both cars move the same way. In C and D a fixed pivot on the push strip locks it.

steps: Work by family: strings (guitars, violin, mandolin), brass (trumpets, horn, tuba, trombone), others (piano, triangle, saxophone, drum).
Trace each outline where instruments overlap.
Tick each instrument as you count it.
The total is 27.
qs.trap: Missing small instruments like triangles, or counting one guitar twice where its neck is hidden.

steps: 1st: a plain, clean e: Reliance.
2nd: an e with a tilted crossbar: Google.
3rd: an e with a bar above it, like an accent: Nestlé.
4th: a wide, flowing italic e: Acer.
qs.trap: Choosing C because Google is the most familiar. Look for the one detail that is unique to each logo.

steps: Start with wings fully up (1).
The wings sweep down: up and back (4), then level with the body (2).
Wings fully down (5).
The wings recover upward (3), ready to repeat frame 1.

steps: Dokra (Dhokra) is lost-wax metal casting by tribal craftspeople of Chhattisgarh, Odisha, West Bengal and Jharkhand.
Its fine thread-like surface comes from wax threads wound on the model.
Bidriware is silver inlay on dark metal (Karnataka). Thewa is gold work on glass (Rajasthan).
Filigree is fine twisted wire (Cuttack).

steps: Tweezers: joined at one end (fulcrum), pressed in the middle (effort), grip at the tips (load): F-E-L.
Nutcracker: hinge at one end (fulcrum), nut in the middle (load), hands at the far end (effort): E-L-F.
So Tweezer = FEL and Nutcracker = ELF.
This is option B.

steps: The pipe under the bowl has a U-bend (or S-bend) that always holds some water.
This water forms a seal between the bathroom and the sewer.
It stops bad-smelling and harmful sewer gases from flowing back into the room.
Flushing uses fresh water from the cistern, so B is not the main purpose.
